    from furl import furl
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    parser.add_argument('--a', type=str, required=True)
    parser.add_argument('--b', type=str, required=True)
    parser.add_argument('--c', type=str, required=True)
    args = parser.parse_args()
    f = furl(args.a)
    print(f.scheme)
    print(f.host)
    print(f.path)
    print(f.query.add({args.b: args.c}))
    print(f.url)

Invoke it as:  /workspace/dataset/test6_executable --a "<URL>" --b "<KEY>" --c "<VAL>"
All three args are REQUIRED. It prints exactly 5 lines:
  line1 = f.scheme      (Python None prints as "None"; empty string prints as "")
  line2 = f.host
  line3 = f.path
  line4 = str(f.query) AFTER add({b: c})
  line5 = f.url AFTER that mutation

PROBING TECHNIQUE:
- Use a bash helper so output is unambiguous. Example:
    p(){ echo "IN=[$1] b=[$2] c=[$3]"; /workspace/dataset/test6_executable --a "$1" --b "$2" --c "$3" 2>&1 | cat -A; echo "rc=$?"; }
  cat -A makes trailing spaces / CR / non-ascii visible ($ = end of line, M- sequences = high bytes).
- Use single quotes in bash to avoid shell mangling.
- To distinguish "empty string" from "None" on a line: cat -A shows "$" for empty and "None$" for None.
- Note lines 4 and 5 reflect the MUTATION (the added b=c pair). To see the *original* query you must
  reason by subtracting the appended pair, or use a b/c pair you can recognize (e.g. b=Z c=Z).
- Some inputs may make the program CRASH (traceback) or exit nonzero. Record those exactly:
  the exception type and message matter, but for our port we mainly need to know WHICH inputs crash.
- Run MANY probes (30+). Be systematic: vary one thing at a time. Confirm every rule with at least
  two independent examples, and actively try to FALSIFY each rule you form.

OUTPUT CONTRACT: return findings as structured data. Rules must be precise enough that another engineer
can implement them in JavaScript WITHOUT running the executable. Always attach the literal probe
transcripts (exact argv you passed, exact 5 output lines) that justify each rule.

line4 is print(f.query.add({key: value})) — the printed object is what add() RETURNS.

Probe --a "http://h/p?K=1" --b K --c 2  -> is line4 "K=1&K=2" or "K=2"?
Probe an empty key: --b "" --c V ; and an empty value: --b K --c "" ; and both empty.
Probe a key that is only "=" or only "&". Probe when the original URL has NO query at all
(is line4 just "K=V" with no leading "&"?) and when the original query is empty ("http://h/p?").
Determine the exact string form of a pair whose value is empty: "K=" or "K"? And a pair whose key is
empty: "=V"? Determine whether the added pair also shows up in line5 and in what position
(before or after the fragment; before or after existing pairs).
Also determine whether the ORIGINAL query pairs get re-encoded when re-serialized (compare
--a "http://h/p?x=a%2Bb" and --a "http://h/p?x=a+b" and --a "http://h/p?x=a b").

content.text: I have comprehensive data. Compiling findings.

input.dimension: query.add({b: c}) semantics and its return value

rules.rule: add() APPENDS, never replaces. Even if the key already exists (once or many times, with or without a value), a new pair is appended and all pre-existing pairs are kept in their original order. There is no de-duplication, not even when the added key AND value are byte-identical to an existing pair.
rules.evidence: argv: --a 'http://h/p?K=1' --b K --c 2 -> [http | h | /p | K=1&K=2 | http://h/p?K=1&K=2]. argv: --a 'http://h/p?x=1&x=2&x=3' --b x --c 4 -> [http | h | /p | x=1&x=2&x=3&x=4 | http://h/p?x=1&x=2&x=3&x=4]. argv: --a 'http://h/p?K=1' --b K --c 1 -> [http | h | /p | K=1&K=1 | http://h/p?K=1&K=1]. argv: --a 'http://h/p?a=1&a' --b a --c z -> [http | h | /p | a=1&a&a=z | http://h/p?a=1&a&a=z]

rules.rule: The new pair is always appended at the very END of the pair list (after every existing pair, including empty/valueless ones). Existing pair order is never reordered or sorted.
rules.evidence: argv: --a 'http://h/p?z=9' --b a --c 1 -> [http | h | /p | z=9&a=1 | http://h/p?z=9&a=1] (not sorted). argv: --a 'http://h/p?b=2&a=1' --b Z --c Z -> [http | h | /p | b=2&a=1&Z=Z | http://h/p?b=2&a=1&Z=Z]. argv: --a 'http://h/p?a=1&' --b Z --c Z -> [http | h | /p | a=1&&Z=Z | http://h/p?a=1&&Z=Z]

rules.rule: add() returns the SAME query object it mutated (self), so line4 == str(f.query) after mutation, and line4 is always exactly the substring of line5 between the '?' and the '#' (or end of string). Implement line4 and line5's query component from one shared serialization.
rules.evidence: Holds in every one of ~60 probes. e.g. argv: --a 'https://u:pw@h:8080/p?a=1#fr' --b Z --c Z -> [https | h | /p | a=1&Z=Z | https://u:pw@h:8080/p?a=1&Z=Z#fr]. argv: --a 'http://h/p?a=1#f?q=2' --b Z --c Z -> [http | h | /p | a=1&Z=Z | http://h/p?a=1&Z=Z#f?q=2]

rules.rule: The ADDED pair is ALWAYS serialized as `encKey` + '=' + `encValue`. The '=' is always emitted, even when the value is the empty string. So: empty value -> 'K=' (never bare 'K'); empty key -> '=V'; both empty -> '='.
rules.evidence: argv: --a 'http://h/p?a=1' --b K --c '' -> [http | h | /p | a=1&K= | http://h/p?a=1&K=]. argv: --a 'http://h/p?a=1' --b '' --c V -> [http | h | /p | a=1&=V | http://h/p?a=1&=V]. argv: --a 'http://h/p?a=1' --b '' --c '' -> [http | h | /p | a=1&= | http://h/p?a=1&=]. argv: --a 'http://h/p' --b '' --c '' -> [http | h | /p | = | http://h/p?=]

rules.rule: When the original URL has NO query at all, or an empty query ('?'), line4 is just the encoded pair with NO leading '&', and line5 becomes url + '?' + pair. '?' with nothing after it means ZERO pairs (not one empty pair).
rules.evidence: argv: --a 'http://h/p' --b K --c V -> [http | h | /p | K=V | http://h/p?K=V]. argv: --a 'http://h/p?' --b K --c V -> [http | h | /p | K=V | http://h/p?K=V]. argv: --a 'http://h' --b Z --c Z -> [http | h | (empty) | Z=Z | http://h?Z=Z]. argv: --a '?' --b Z --c Z -> [None | None | (empty) | Z=Z | ?Z=Z]

rules.rule: Pairs are joined with '&' only. Serialization is: for each pair, (key===None-valued ? encKey : encKey + '=' + encValue), joined by '&'.
rules.evidence: argv: --a 'http://h/p?a=1&b' --b Z --c Z -> [http | h | /p | a=1&b&Z=Z | http://h/p?a=1&b&Z=Z] (valueless 'b' stays bare). argv: --a 'http://h/p?b&a=1' --b Z --c Z -> [http | h | /p | b&a=1&Z=Z | http://h/p?b&a=1&Z=Z]

rules.rule: ENCODER (used identically for the added key, the added value, and every re-serialized original key/value): UTF-8 encode the string; for each byte, output the literal char if it is A-Z a-z 0-9 or one of '-' '.' '_' '~'; output '+' for space (0x20); otherwise output '%' + two UPPERCASE hex digits. This is Python quote_plus with safe=''. Note '!' '*' '(' ')' "'" are NOT safe (unlike JS encodeURIComponent).
rules.evidence: Full ASCII sweep on the value (--a 'http://h/p' --b K --c 'X<ch>X', line4 shown): !->X%21X "->X%22X #->X%23X $->X%24X %->X%25X &->X%26X '->X%27X (->X%28X )->X%29X *->X%2AX +->X%2BX ,->X%2CX -->X-X .->X.X /->X%2FX :->X%3AX ;->X%3BX <->X%3CX =->X%3DX >->X%3EX ?->X%3FX @->X%40X [->X%5BX \->X%5CX ]->X%5DX ^->X%5EX _->X_X `->X%60X {->X%7BX |->X%7CX }->X%7DX ~->X~X space->X+X. Same for keys: --a 'http://h/p' --b 'K*K' --c V -> line4 'K%2AK=V'; --b 'K~K' -> 'K~K=V'; --b 'K K' -> 'K+K=V'; --b 'K+K' -> 'K%2BK=V'. Full transcript example: argv --a 'http://h/p' --b K --c ':@$,;' -> [http | h | /p | K=%3A%40%24%2C%3B | http://h/p?K=%3A%40%24%2C%3B]

rules.rule: Non-ASCII in key or value is UTF-8 encoded then percent-encoded byte-by-byte (uppercase hex). Control chars likewise (\n -> %0A, \t -> %09).
rules.evidence: argv: --a 'http://h/p' --b K --c 'é' -> [http | h | /p | K=%C3%A9 | http://h/p?K=%C3%A9]. argv: --a 'http://h/p' --b K --c '日本' -> [http | h | /p | K=%E6%97%A5%E6%9C%AC | http://h/p?K=%E6%97%A5%E6%9C%AC]. argv: --a 'http://h/p' --b 'é' --c V -> [http | h | /p | %C3%A9=V | http://h/p?%C3%A9=V]. argv: --a 'http://h/p' --b K --c 'ü ö' -> [http | h | /p | K=%C3%BC+%C3%B6 | http://h/p?K=%C3%BC+%C3%B6]

rules.rule: The key/value strings are treated as LITERAL text, not pre-encoded. A '%' the caller passes is escaped to '%25' (double-encoding), and '=' / '&' / '#' / '?' inside the key or value are escaped so they can never break out of their pair.
rules.evidence: argv: --a 'http://h/p' --b K --c '%2F' -> [http | h | /p | K=%252F | http://h/p?K=%252F]. argv: --a 'http://h/p' --b K --c '%41' -> [http | h | /p | K=%2541 | http://h/p?K=%2541]. argv: --a 'http://h/p?a=1' --b Z --c '%3F' -> [http | h | /p | a=1&Z=%253F | http://h/p?a=1&Z=%253F]. argv: --a 'http://h/p' --b K --c 'a&b=c' -> [http | h | /p | K=a%26b%3Dc | http://h/p?K=a%26b%3Dc]. argv: --a 'http://h/p?a=1' --b '&Z=1&' --c V -> [http | h | /p | a=1&%26Z%3D1%26=V | http://h/p?a=1&%26Z%3D1%26=V]

rules.rule: ORIGINAL query pairs ARE re-encoded: each original key/value is percent-DECODED (with '+' -> space) and then re-encoded with the same encoder as rule 7. Consequences: '%20' -> '+', a raw space -> '+', a literal '+' stays '+', '%2B' stays '%2B', '%7E' -> '~', '%41' -> 'A', lowercase hex is uppercased ('%2f' -> '%2F'), '%2F'/'%3A'/'%26'/'%3D'/'%23' stay percent-encoded.
rules.evidence: argv: --a 'http://h/p?x=a%2Bb' --b Z --c Z -> [http | h | /p | x=a%2Bb&Z=Z | http://h/p?x=a%2Bb&Z=Z]. argv: --a 'http://h/p?x=a+b' --b Z --c Z -> [http | h | /p | x=a+b&Z=Z | http://h/p?x=a+b&Z=Z]. argv: --a 'http://h/p?x=a b' --b Z --c Z -> [http | h | /p | x=a+b&Z=Z | http://h/p?x=a+b&Z=Z]. argv: --a 'http://h/p?x=a%20b' --b Z --c Z -> [http | h | /p | x=a+b&Z=Z | http://h/p?x=a+b&Z=Z]. argv: --a 'http://h/p?x=%7E%2F%3A' --b Z --c Z -> [http | h | /p | x=~%2F%3A&Z=Z | http://h/p?x=~%2F%3A&Z=Z]. argv: --a 'http://h/p?x=%41%42%30' --b Z --c Z -> [http | h | /p | x=AB0&Z=Z | http://h/p?x=AB0&Z=Z]. argv: --a 'http://h/p?%2f' --b Z --c Z -> [http | h | /p | %2F&Z=Z | http://h/p?%2F&Z=Z]

rules.rule: Malformed percent escapes in the original query ('%' not followed by two hex digits) are decoded as a LITERAL '%' character and therefore re-encoded to '%25'.
rules.evidence: argv: --a 'http://h/p?x=%' --b Z --c Z -> [http | h | /p | x=%25&Z=Z | http://h/p?x=%25&Z=Z]. argv: --a 'http://h/p?x=%zz' --b Z --c Z -> [http | h | /p | x=%25zz&Z=Z | http://h/p?x=%25zz&Z=Z]. argv: --a 'http://h/p?x=%2' --b Z --c Z -> [http | h | /p | x=%252&Z=Z | http://h/p?x=%252&Z=Z]

rules.rule: Original query parsing: split ONLY on '&' (';' is NOT a separator). Each segment is split at its FIRST '=' -> (key, value); any further '=' belong to the value and get re-encoded as '%3D'. A segment containing no '=' has value None and re-serializes as the bare encoded key (no trailing '='). A segment that is exactly '' yields an empty key with value None and re-serializes as ''.
rules.evidence: argv: --a 'http://h/p?a=1;b=2' --b Z --c Z -> [http | h | /p | a=1%3Bb%3D2&Z=Z | http://h/p?a=1%3Bb%3D2&Z=Z] (one pair, ';' not a separator). argv: --a 'http://h/p?a=1=2' --b Z --c Z -> [http | h | /p | a=1%3D2&Z=Z | http://h/p?a=1%3D2&Z=Z]. argv: --a 'http://h/p?a=1?b=2' --b Z --c Z -> [http | h | /p | a=1%3Fb%3D2&Z=Z | http://h/p?a=1%3Fb%3D2&Z=Z]. argv: --a 'http://h/p?x' --b Z --c Z -> [http | h | /p | x&Z=Z | http://h/p?x&Z=Z]. argv: --a 'http://h/p?x=' --b Z --c Z -> [http | h | /p | x=&Z=Z | http://h/p?x=&Z=Z]

rules.rule: Empty segments from '&&', a leading '&' or a trailing '&' are preserved as empty pairs, so the '&' runs survive the round-trip and the added pair still goes after them.
rules.evidence: argv: --a 'http://h/p?a=1&&b=2' --b Z --c Z -> [http | h | /p | a=1&&b=2&Z=Z | http://h/p?a=1&&b=2&Z=Z]. argv: --a 'http://h/p?&' --b Z --c Z -> [http | h | /p | &&Z=Z | http://h/p?&&Z=Z]. argv: --a 'http://h/p?&a=1' --b Z --c Z -> [http | h | /p | &a=1&Z=Z | http://h/p?&a=1&Z=Z]. argv: --a 'http://h/p?a=1&' --b Z --c Z -> [http | h | /p | a=1&&Z=Z | http://h/p?a=1&&Z=Z]

rules.rule: In line5 the added pair lands inside the QUERY component: after the path, after all existing pairs, and BEFORE the '#fragment'. If the URL previously had no query, a '?' is inserted before the fragment. Text that looks like a query but sits inside the fragment ('#f?q=1') is left in the fragment and is NOT merged.
rules.evidence: argv: --a 'http://h/p?a=1#frag' --b Z --c Z -> [http | h | /p | a=1&Z=Z | http://h/p?a=1&Z=Z#frag]. argv: --a 'http://h/p#f?q=1' --b Z --c Z -> [http | h | /p | Z=Z | http://h/p?Z=Z#f?q=1]. argv: --a '#f' --b Z --c Z -> [None | None | (empty) | Z=Z | ?Z=Z#f]

rules.rule: add() itself never raises for any string key/value (including '', '=', '&', '#', '%', newlines, non-ASCII). Every nonzero-exit observed came from URL parsing of --a before add() ran (e.g. 'ValueError: Invalid IPv6 URL', "ValueError: Invalid port '99999'."), producing a traceback on stderr and rc=1 with zero of the 5 lines printed.
rules.evidence: argv: --a 'http://[bad?a=1' --b Z --c Z -> traceback ending 'ValueError: Invalid IPv6 URL', rc=1, no output lines. argv: --a 'http://h:99999/p?a=1' --b Z --c Z -> traceback ending "ValueError: Invalid port '99999'.", rc=1. Contrast: argv --a 'http://h/p' --b '&' --c '&' -> [http | h | /p | %26=%26 | http://h/p?%26=%26] rc=0; argv --a 'http://h/p' --b '=' --c '=' -> [http | h | /p | %3D=%3D | http://h/p?%3D=%3D] rc=0

uncertainties: I could not pass a literal NUL byte through argv, so the encoding of \x00 in the ADDED key/value is untested (an original '%00' in the URL round-trips as '%00', so '%00' is the likely output).

Whether the internal representation distinguishes 'value is None' vs 'value is empty string' is inferred only from serialization: original segments without '=' print bare (e.g. 'x'), original segments with '=' print 'x='. The added pair always has a string value, so it always prints 'k=v'. I could not construct an added pair with a None value from the CLI (argparse type=str always yields a string).

Bytes 0x80-0xFF that are not valid UTF-8 cannot be passed via argv reliably, so behavior of the original query containing invalid-UTF-8 percent escapes (e.g. '?x=%FF') was not probed. '%C3%A9' round-trips unchanged, which suggests decode-to-text then re-encode, but a lone '%FF' may behave differently (surrogateescape) — untested.
Very long keys/values (>8KB) were not probed for truncation; no reason to expect any.

Whether a trailing '#' with an empty fragment is dropped from line5 was observed once ('http://h/p?a=1#' -> line5 'http://h/p?a=1&Z=Z', no '#'), but that belongs to the fragment dimension and was only tested once here.
